title: The Concept of Social Stratification
text:
Social stratification refers to a society’s classification into distinct, hierarchical layers. These inequalities are patterned and enduring across generations, determined by factors such as wealth, occupation, and social status. The mechanisms supporting this structure include ascribed statuses (those assigned at birth) and achieved statuses (those earned through effort).

Theoretical frameworks analyze the roots of stratification differently. Functionalist perspectives argue that stratification is necessary because differential rewards incentivize individuals to perform roles critical to societal maintenance. In contrast, conflict theory posits that stratification is primarily a result of power dynamics and institutional control exercised by dominant groups over subordinate ones.

Modern sociological analysis also examines intersectionality, which recognizes that systems of oppression are not linear. An individual's experiences of disadvantage or privilege result from the complex interplay between race, class, gender, sexuality, and other identities, creating overlapping axes of inequality.
